hints: Compare the functional groups in $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$ and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ and think about gain of hydrogen versus gain of oxygen.
walkthrough:
Track what happens to the functional group**
Look closely at reaction 1. You start with a carboxylic acid, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$, and you finish with a primary alcohol, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. The $\text{C=O}$ has become $\text{CH}_2$, so oxygen has been removed and hydrogen has been added.

Link to the definition**
Gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen is reduction. So converting a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol is a reduction.

hints: Recall which reagents replace the $\text{-OH}$ group of an alcohol with $\text{-Cl}$ without changing the carbon skeleton.
walkthrough:
Spot the functional group change**
Reaction 2 goes from $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ to $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$. Only $\text{OH}$ is swapped for $\text{Cl}$. This is nucleophilic substitution of $\text{OH}$ by $\text{Cl}$.

Choose the chlorinating agent**
$\text{OH}$ is a poor leaving group, so you need a reagent that provides $\text{Cl}$ and removes $\text{OH}$. At AS level the standard choices are $\text{PCl}_5$, $\text{PCl}_3$, $\text{SOCl}_2$, or $\text{NaCl}$ with concentrated acid.
Final answer: $\text{PCl}_5$ or $\text{PCl}_3$ or $\text{SOCl}_2$ or $\text{NaCl}$ / $\text{KCl}$ with conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ / conc. $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$

hints: Think about what small molecules are lost when a chloroalkane forms an alkene with $\text{NaOH}$, and why the solvent matters.
Recall the difference between aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ which gives substitution and the alternative $\text{NaOH}$ conditions which favour elimination.
walkthrough:
Write the elimination equation**
In reaction 3, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ loses $\text{HCl}$ to form $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$. With $\text{NaOH}$ this becomes: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_3\text{H}_6 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{NaCl}$$ Check atoms: $\text{C}_3$, $\text{H}_8$, $\text{O}_1$, $\text{Na}_1$, $\text{Cl}_1$ on both sides.

Pick conditions that favour elimination**
$\text{NaOH}$ can do two jobs. In water it substitutes $\text{Cl}$ for $\text{OH}$. In ethanol with heat it acts as a base and removes $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ together. So you must state ethanol as solvent with heat or reflux.

Final answer: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_3\text{H}_6 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{NaCl}$
ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$, heat / reflux

hints: Remember the standard way to remove water directly from an alcohol to make an alkene, think concentrated acid or hot solid catalyst.
walkthrough:
Recognise direct dehydration**
Going straight from $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ to $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$ means losing $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ from the alcohol. This is acid catalysed dehydration, an elimination.

Name the dehydrating conditions**
The classic reagents are concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ or concentrated $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ with heat, or passing the vapour over hot $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$.
Final answer: conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ or conc. $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ or $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, with heat

hints: Think about whether propene joining to itself to make poly(propene) loses any small molecule or simply adds across the $\text{C=C}$ bond.
walkthrough:
Check the monomer and polymer**
Propene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$, is an alkene. When many propene molecules join, the $\text{C=C}$ double bond opens and each monomer simply adds to the chain with no other product lost.

Name the type**
Polymerisation with no small molecule lost and involving an unsaturated monomer is addition polymerisation.

hints: Start by recalling what stays the same in any type of isomerism, think about atoms present and how they are connected.
Now focus on what makes stereo different from structural, think about arrangement in 3D space rather than connectivity.
walkthrough:
State what is identical**
Stereoisomers have the same atoms joined in the same order. That means they share the same molecular formula and the same structural formula.

State what is different**
What differs is how those atoms or groups are arranged in 3D space. That different spatial arrangement cannot be interconverted by rotation and gives different stereoisomers.
Final answer: Molecules with the same structural formula (and same molecular formula) but with a different three-dimensional / spatial arrangement of atoms / groups.

hints: Draw propene $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$ opening its double bond, then join two of these units head to tail to show the backbone.
Look for a carbon in the polymer chain bonded to four different groups, and recall which type of stereoisomerism needs this feature.
Check the carbon bearing the methyl group in your drawn section and list its four attachments to justify your choice.
walkthrough:
Draw two repeat units correctly**
Open the $\text{C=C}$ in propene. Each propene gives $\text{ - CH}_2\text{ - CH(CH}_3\text{) - }$. Join two together head to tail: $$\text{ - CH}_2\text{ - CH(CH}_3\text{) - CH}_2\text{ - CH(CH}_3\text{) - }$$ Show the side $\text{CH}_3$ groups clearly and put continuation bonds at each end to show the chain continues.

Identify optical isomerism**
Poly(propene) cannot show cis-trans isomerism because there is no $\text{C=C}$ left. Instead, the $\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}$ carbon is chiral. Different chains can have the $\text{CH}_3$ groups arranged differently in space, giving non-superimposable arrangements. This is optical isomerism.

Explain the chiral centre**
Look at that methyl-bearing carbon. It is attached to: $\text{H}$, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_2$ on one side of the chain, and $\text{CH}_2$ on the other side leading to different chain lengths in a longer polymer. Four different groups means it is a chiral centre, which allows optical isomers.

Final answer: Section: $\text{ - CH}_2\text{ - CH(CH}_3\text{) - CH}_2\text{ - CH(CH}_3\text{) - }$ with continuation bonds shown.
Type: optical isomerism.
Reason: the carbon attached to the methyl group ($\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}$) is bonded to four different groups.

hints: Think about what happens if poly(propene) is left in landfill, consider whether microorganisms can break strong C-C polymer chains.
Think about what happens if poly(propene) is burned instead, consider the gases formed by incomplete combustion of a hydrocarbon polymer.
walkthrough:
Landfill problem**
Poly(propene) has long, non-polar $\text{C-C}$ chains that microorganisms cannot digest. So it is non-biodegradable. It stays in landfill for many years, taking up space.

Burning problem**
As a hydrocarbon polymer, burning it, especially in limited oxygen, gives harmful products such as carbon monoxide, $\text{CO}$, unburnt hydrocarbons and soot particles, which are toxic and polluting. Even complete combustion releases large amounts of $\text{CO}_2$.

Final answer: 1. Non-biodegradable / persists in landfill, causes visual pollution and waste accumulation.
2. Combustion produces harmful / toxic gases e.g. $\text{CO}$ and soot, contributing to air pollution.

hints: Find the longest chain containing the double bond in X, number it to give the double bond the lowest number, then locate the methyl branches.
walkthrough:
Name structure X**
X has a $\text{C=C}$ at the end with structure $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3\text{)CH(CH}_3\text{)}_2$? Actually draw it: $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3\text{)-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_3$. The longest chain through the double bond has 4 carbons, so it is a butene with the double bond starting at carbon 1.

Add substituents**
There is a methyl on carbon 2 and a methyl on carbon 3. Numbering from the double bond end gives 2,3-dimethylbut-1-ene.

hints: Compare the structures of X ($\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3\text{)CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_3$) and Y ($\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=C(CH}_3\text{)}_2$ type) and think which fragments at m/e 41, 43, 42 or 54 each one can easily form.
walkthrough:
Use the molecular ion and fragments**
Both X and Y are $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}$, $M_r = 84$, so the peak near m/e 84 is the molecular ion for either. You must use fragmentation to tell them apart.

Match fragments to X**
X is $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3\text{)CH(CH}_3\text{CH}_3$. Cleavage can give $[\text{CH}_2\text{=CCH}_3]^+$ at m/e 41 and $[\text{CH}_3\text{CHCH}_3]^+$ at m/e 43, both seen as large peaks in Fig. 4.2. Y, which is more symmetrical $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=C(CH}_3)_2$ type, would be expected to show peaks at 54 and 42 instead. So the spectrum matches X.

Final answer: The spectrum is of X because peak at m/e 41 is $[\text{CH}_2\text{=CCH}_3]^+$ / $\text{C}_3\text{H}_5^+$ or peak at m/e 43 is $[\text{CH}_3\text{CHCH}_3]^+$ / $\text{C}_3\text{H}_7^+$ (fragments that X can form but Y cannot readily form).

hints: Recall that the height of the $[\text{M}+1]^+$ peak depends on the number of carbon atoms and the 1.1 percent natural abundance of $^{13}\text{C}$.
walkthrough:
Count carbons for the isotope calculation**
X and Y are $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}$, so there are 6 carbons. Each carbon has about a 1.1 percent chance of being $^{13}\text{C}$.

Calculate the expected abundance**
Relative abundance of $[\text{M}+1]^+$ is: $$\text{abundance} = \frac{34.7 \times 6 \times 1.1}{100} = 2.29$$ So the $[\text{M}+1]^+$ peak has relative abundance about 2.29.
